content: The term dandelion refers to species within the genus Taraxacum, a large group of flowering plants belonging to the family Asteraceae. In this family, what appears to be a single flower is actually a composite flower head made up of numerous small flowers called florets. Dandelions are native to Europe and Asia but have spread widely to other regions. In areas where they are not native, particularly in northern climates, they are often considered invasive weeds, thriving in disturbed soils and human-altered environments. Dandelions reproduce asexually through a process called apomixis, allowing them to produce seeds without pollination. Dandelions are herbaceous plants with a taproot system and can be biennial or perennial. They are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Commonly regarded as weeds, they are also classified as ruderals, meaning they thrive in disturbed habitats. The genus Taraxacum is taxonomically complex, with many species exhibiting polyploidy. Over 250 species have been identified in the British Isles alone, though some botanists recognize only about 60 species. The leaves of dandelions are simple, basal, and form a rosette above the central taproot. They range from 5 to 25 cm in length and may be entire or lobed. As the leaves grow outward, they suppress surrounding vegetation, such as grass, by blocking sunlight. The plant produces bright yellow flower heads, which open during the day and close at night. These flower heads are borne singly on hollow stems (scapes) that exude a milky latex when broken. Each rosette can produce multiple flowering stems, which rise 4 to 30 cm above the leaves. The flower head, measuring 2 to 5 cm in diameter, consists entirely of ray florets. Dandelions serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species. Outside their native range, dandelions have become established as weeds in the Americas, Australia, and New Zealand, and they are now widespread in temperate regions worldwide. When the flower matures, it transforms into a spherical structure composed of fine filaments that facilitate wind dispersal of the seed-containing achenes. This structure is commonly referred to as the dandelion clock. The flower head is surrounded by bracts, often mistaken for sepals, arranged in two series. The inner bracts remain upright until the seeds mature, after which they bend downward to allow seed dispersal. The outer bracts are always reflexed downward. Some species shed the parachute-like structure, known as the pappus, from the achenes. Between the pappus and the achene is a stalk called the beak, which elongates as the fruit matures and detaches easily from the achene. The name dandelion originates from the French term dent-de-lion, meaning lion's tooth, a reference to the plant's sharply lobed leaves. The English spelling reflects the French pronunciation at the time the word was adopted into English. The earliest recorded use of the term dates back to a 1373 herbal text, though it also appeared as a proper name in a 1363 document. In other languages, the name often translates to lion's tooth, such as Löwenzahn in German, diente de león in Spanish, and dente-de-leão in Portuguese. In Norwegian, it is called Løvetann, and in Turkish, it is known as karahindiba, meaning black endive. Folk names in various languages often reference the plant's diuretic properties, such as pissabeds in English and piscialletto in Italian. Several species of dandelions are notable, including Taraxacum officinale (common dandelion), Taraxacum albidum (a white-flowering Japanese dandelion), Taraxacum japonicum (a Japanese dandelion lacking a ring of downward-turned leaves beneath the flower head), and Taraxacum laevigatum (red-seeded dandelion, characterized by reddish-brown achenes and deeply cut leaves). The genus Taraxacum is genetically complex, with many species being triploid. Triploidy, which involves an odd number of chromosomes, typically results in sterility. However, triploid dandelions can reproduce asexually through apomixis, bypassing the need for fertilization. In these cases, flowers are vestigial structures, though they may still produce a small amount of fertile pollen, allowing limited genetic exchange with sexually reproducing individuals. Diploid dandelions, on the other hand, require cross-pollination and are self-incompatible. In southern Europe and Asia, dandelion populations are often sexual or mixed sexual-apomictic, whereas in northern regions and non-native areas, only triploid and tetraploid apomicts are typically found. This distribution may be influenced by factors such as temperature, pre-glacial population survival, and human activity. A single dandelion flower head can produce 54 to 172 seeds, and a single plant may yield over 2,000 seeds annually. In dense stands, dandelions can produce an estimated 97 million seeds per hectare each year. After pollination, the dandelion flower dries over approximately 10 days, during which the seed-bearing parachutes expand and lift out of the dried flower head. The dried flower parts fall away, and the parachute ball opens into a full sphere. When the seeds are released, the parachutes lose their feathered structure and take on a fuzzy, cotton-like appearance, often referred to as dandelion snow. Seeds frequently germinate near obstacles, such as walls, where the wind-blown fruits strike and drop their pappi. Despite being considered a weed, dandelions have culinary and medicinal uses. They are cultivated on a small scale as a leaf vegetable and can be consumed raw or cooked. Young leaves and unopened buds are often eaten raw in salads, while older leaves are cooked. The raw leaves have a slightly bitter taste and are rich in vitamins A and C, as well as iron and calcium, surpassing spinach in iron and calcium content. Dandelion flowers are used to make wine, often with the addition of citrus fruits, and can also be made into jam. Roasted dandelion roots serve as a coffee substitute and are believed to stimulate digestion when consumed before meals. Dandelion root is a registered diuretic in Canada and is considered a liver tonic. The plant's latex has been used as a mosquito repellent and as a treatment for warts. Additionally, a dye can be extracted from the roots. Products such as DandyBlend, made from roasted dandelion roots, mimic the taste of coffee. In the United Kingdom, a traditional soft drink called Dandelion and Burdock is sold, though it is unclear if modern versions contain the actual plants. Dandelions contain luteolin, a compound with antioxidant properties, and have demonstrated antioxidant activity without cytotoxic effects. They also produce caffeic acid, a secondary plant metabolite unrelated to caffeine. While some studies have suggested that caffeic acid may be carcinogenic in animal models, its effects in humans remain unclear, and no adverse effects have been reported. Dandelions are often confused with similar plants, such as catsears (Hypochoeris), which are also called false dandelions. Catsears have forked, solid stems, whereas dandelions have hollow, unforked stems. Both plants have a rosette of leaves and a central taproot, but dandelion leaves are jagged, while catsear leaves are lobed and hairy. Other plants with similar flowers include hawkweeds (Hieracium) and hawksbeards (Crepis), which can be distinguished by their branched flowering stems.
